title: Multi-tenancy and noisy neighbours
subtitle: Many customers share one system. Learn to keep their data apart and stop one busy customer from slowing down everyone else.

c.v: This story is made up, but it is common. A small company sells invoicing software to 400 businesses. All of them share one set of app servers and one Postgres database. This is cheap and easy to run.
On the last day of the year, the biggest customer starts a full export of five years of invoices. It runs as hundreds of heavy queries at once. The database CPU goes to 100%.
Every other customer now waits 20 seconds to open an invoice. Support gets messages from 399 businesses that did nothing wrong. The
engineer sees "database slow" on the dashboard, but nothing says which customer is causing it.
It takes an hour to find the export and stop it. Then a second question comes: "Could a slow query ever return another customer's invoices?" Nobody is sure. Every query has
, but only because developers remembered to add it.
is one customer organisation, such as one company.
means one running system serves many tenants. The tenants share code, servers and often databases, but each must feel like it has the system to itself.
You must keep tenants apart in two ways:
A tenant must never see another tenant's data. A 2020 AWS whitepaper calls crossing this line "a significant and potentially un-recoverable event" for a SaaS (software as a service) business.
One tenant must not make the system slow for the rest. This is the
problem: one user puts so much load on shared resources that other users suffer.
Sharing makes SaaS cheap. Every shared thing is also a path for a leak or a slowdown. Decide what to share on purpose, and isolate each shared thing.
Each tenant gets its own resources, such as its own database or even its own full stack.
Tenants share resources. This is classic multi-tenancy, and it lowers the cost per tenant as you grow.
A mix. Some services are siloed and others are pooled. Strict data rules or noisy load can push one service to silo. Cost and agility can push another to pool.
The pool is cheapest, because it scales with the real load of all tenants. The same 2020 whitepaper lists its costs too: noisy neighbours, harder cost tracking per tenant, and a bigger
. One outage will likely hit every tenant.

You can mix models by price tier. Basic tenants share a pool, and premium tenants pay for their own stack. A 2022 AWS whitepaper (now archived) adds a warning: every silo should run the same version and setup as the pool, with no one-off changes.
If you skip this, you end up running many different products.

goes one step further. Amazon's example has 8 workers.
, a bad customer can crash all 8 workers. Everyone is down.
With 4 fixed shards of 2 workers, a bad customer crashes one shard. That is 25% of customers.

With shuffle sharding, each customer gets a random pair of workers. There are 28 possible pairs. A bad customer crashes its own pair. Only customers with that exact pair lose everything. The impact drops to 1/28, which Amazon calls 7 times better than plain sharding.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "Where is the tenant id here, and what stops a query without it?"
Write a test that logs in as tenant A and tries to read tenant B's data through every API. Run it in
"What is the most one tenant can use?"
Check requests, connections, jobs, storage and export size.
Put tenant id on every log line and metric, so on-call can see who is noisy and who is hurt.
Keep a list of your largest tenants and their growth. Plan their move to a bigger tier early.
Keep every silo on the same version as the pool. Treat a "special build for one customer" as a warning sign.
Before an incident, know your blast radius: how many tenants share each database, cell and queue.
"Add PostgreSQL row-level security to these tables. Use a policy on tenant_id that reads current_setting('app.current_tenant'). The app role must not own the tables."
"Find every query, cache key and queue message in this service that does not include the tenant id. List them by file and line."
"Write an integration test: log in as tenant A, then call every read endpoint with ids that belong to tenant B. Every call must return 404 or 403."
"Add a per-tenant limit on concurrent export jobs, 2 per tenant, stored in Redis. Log the tenant id and the limit when a job is rejected."
The app connects as a role that does not own the tables and does not have BYPASSRLS. Otherwise RLS does nothing.
The tenant id comes from the auth token, not from a header or body the client controls.
The tenant setting is set per transaction and cannot leak to the next request on a pooled connection.
Cache keys, file paths and search indexes include the tenant id, not only database rows.
Limits are per tenant, not global. A global limit lets one tenant use it all.

q.v: Your app runs one shared Postgres database for all tenants. What protects you best if a developer forgets a tenant filter in one query?

options.v: Row-level security on the table, with the app connecting as a role that is not the table owner.

why.v: Row-level security adds the tenant filter inside the database, for every query. The table owner skips it by default, so the app must use another role.

q.v: Which model gives the strongest isolation, at the highest cost per tenant?

why.v: In the silo model each tenant gets its own resources. Nothing is shared, but you pay for idle capacity and run many copies.

q.v: You have 8 workers. Each tenant gets a random pair of 2 workers (shuffle sharding). How many different pairs are there?

why.v: There are 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 pairs. A bad tenant takes down its own pair. Another tenant loses both workers only if it has the exact same pair.

q.v: One tenant's traffic grows 50 times in an hour. What should stop it from hurting the others first?

options.v: A per-tenant quota or rate limit that rejects the extra requests early.
Waiting for autoscaling to add servers.
Moving every tenant to its own database tonight.

why.v: A per-tenant limit rejects the extra requests at once and affects only that tenant. Autoscaling is slower and shares the new capacity with the noisy tenant.

q.v: Why should you log the tenant id on every request?

options.v: So you can see which tenant uses the most capacity, and who is affected in an incident.
Because the database needs it to run queries.

why.v: Without the tenant id, a dashboard shows "the system is slow" but not "tenant 42 is causing it" or "tenants 7 and 9 are hurt".
